input: This staffing review examines the position in a dispatch office which employs 11 full-time members of staff and which recorded overtime amounting to 6% of paid hours over the course of last year. It is important to appreciate that this overtime is not spread evenly across the year as a whole; rather, it is concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks, and between those peaks the office's paid hours are perfectly adequately covered by the existing staff, with no overtime arising at all. One option that has been put forward is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, which would cost $69k per year on a fully loaded basis, the half in question being equivalent to 3% of paid hours. However, any such hire would be paid for the full year, which means that the salary would continue to run through the quieter months as well as through the peaks, whereas the overtime that it replaces is purchased only in the weeks in which peak demand actually arises. The remaining half of the overtime would, of course, still remain in place under this option, and the peaks would continue to be worked partly on overtime. Overall, the comparison that the review presents is essentially between a fixed annual salary commitment and a variable cost that follows the pattern of demand across the year, together with the additional consideration that a hire would provide extra capacity in ordinary weeks, absorbing absence, leave and training without recourse to overtime, a benefit which the stated figure of $69k does not itself price. The decision ultimately rests on the height and duration of the two seasonal peaks, rather than on the annual percentage share of overtime in total paid hours.
target: A dispatch office employing 11 full-time staff recorded overtime at 6% of paid hours last year. The overtime falls in two seasonal peaks and is absent between them, when the office's paid hours are covered by the existing staff. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $69k per year fully loaded; the half replaced is 3% of paid hours. A hire is paid for the full year, so the salary runs through the quiet months as well as the peaks, while the overtime it replaces is bought only in the weeks where the peak demand arises. The other half of the overtime remains under this option, and the peaks would still be worked partly on overtime, at the times of year when the office is under most pressure. The comparison the review sets out is a fixed annual salary against a cost that follows the demand curve of the office's year. What the hire adds beyond peak cover is capacity in every ordinary week: absence, leave and training are absorbed without recourse to overtime, and the office carries a margin it does not have at present. That margin has a value the stated figures do not price, and it is not part of the comparison as costed. On the stated figures, the $69k buys out half of a peak-concentrated overtime bill at the price of a year-round commitment, and the case turns on the height and length of the two peaks rather than on the annual share of overtime in paid hours.
